list.listitem: Complex regional pain syndrome (CRPS) is a rare disorder that typically develops four to six weeks after direct trauma, such as an injury or surgery; pain is usually out of proportion to the inciting injury. C
The diagnosis is clinical using the Budapest diagnostic criteria and tests should be performed to rule out alternative diagnoses. C

No single treatment modality has been found to be helpful for CRPS, and the main goal of therapy is to improve function of the affected body part and to minimize pain through multiple modalities, including behavioral health interventions and medications used to treat neuropathic pain.. A

Based on two randomized trials, research, daily administration of 500-1000 mg of Vitamin C reduces the risk of developing of CRPS-I following trauma of the upper or lower extremities and following orthopedic surgery. B

Good-quality evidence shows a decrease in CRPS pain with bisphosphonates. Steroids might be helpful in the acute phase, while NSAIDS are likely of no benefit. Ketamine may also be helpful in selected patients. B

background.definition: Complex regional pain syndrome (CRPS) is a rare disorder that typically develops four to six weeks after direct trauma, such as an injury or surgery and pain is usually out of proportion to the inciting injury. CRPS I and CPRS II were previously known as reflex sympathetic dystrophy (RSD) and causalgia. In CRPS II there is an observable nerve injury, while in CRPS I (which accounts for 90% of cases) no nerve involvement is seen on a nerve conduction velocity study. The IASP classifies CRPS as a chronic primary pain disorder, recognizing it as a distinct health condition characterized by persistent pain >3 months with associated emotional distress or functional impairment not better explained by another diagnosis. This classification is etiology-agnostic and formally acknowledges the biopsychosocial mechanisms underlying CRPS. The IASP Valencia adaptations introduce a subtype, CRPS in partial remission, for individuals who previously met Budapest criteria but continue to experience residual signs or symptoms.

list.listitem: One study showed on incidence of 5.5 per 100,000 person years at risk.
Women are more commonly affected than men at a ratio of 4:1, and incidence peaks between 40 and 70 years of age. It is rare in children in whom injuries heal faster
There is a 2-25% incidence following wrist fractures, 26% incidence following traumatic hand injuries and 13% incidence following total knee arthroplasty.
Prevalence of 20.6 per 100,000 persons found in 1 study done in Olmsted County, MN.
Trauma (most common upper extremity fracture).
Medical intervention (surgery, venipuncture).
Visceral trauma.
Stroke.

CRPS risk is influenced by the severity and inflammatory nature of the initial injury, with higher incidence following open fractures and crush injuries compared with minor trauma.¹ Post-injury immobilization (cast or splint) is associated with increased risk, potentially mediated via inflammatory pathways.¹ Across prospective studies, higher early post-traumatic or post-operative pain intensity remains the most consistent predictor of CRPS development.

Most theories suggest CRPS to involve both the central and peripheral nervous systems. There appears to be little relationship between CRPS and psychological factors, although the condition may be related to stressful life events.
Recent studies of minimal distal nerve injury have shown a loss of small-fiber axons in areas with CRPS I.

Emerging evidence supports an immune-mediated inflammatory contribution to CRPS. Acute CRPS is associated with upregulated proinflammatory cytokines in affected tissues and circulation with autoreactive IgM antibodies, while chronic CRPS demonstrates persistent cytokine elevation and IgG antibodies. Alterations in neuropeptides such as bradykinin and substance P, along with impaired metabolism, may contribute to pain and autonomic features via peripheral nociceptor sensitization. Adaptive immune involvement and autoantibody-mediated mechanisms are suggested by animal models. Functional MRI studies indicate that CRPS symptoms may involve impaired central antinociceptive modulation, potentially through dysfunction of the periaqueductal grey and descending inhibitory pathways.
Vitamin C 500 mg daily for 2 months in patients with upper extremity fractures was shown in 2 RCTS to reduce the risk of CRPS (NNT = 7-13). A

Patients typically present with disproportionate pain following injury (commonly extremity fracture) accompanied by allodynia, hyperalgesia, vasomotor and sudomotor changes, weakness, tremor, or atrophy. C
Diagnostic tests such as MRI, radiographs, triple phase bone scan, or thermography are somewhat helpful if abnormal 8 to 16 weeks after injury; normal test does not rule out CRPS. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Pain in a specific dermatome, no recent trauma
Pain in multiple dermatomes, no recent trauma
Characteristic blanching associated with cold exposure

list.listitem: The Budapest criteria developed by the International Association for the Study of Pain is 99% sensitive and 68% specific for CRPS (LR+ 3, LR- 0.02): Pain is disproportionate to an inciting event Patient reports at least 1 symptom in 3 of the 4 following categories: (1) sensory: hypesthesia, allodynia, myofascial pain syndrome; (2) vasomotor: temperature asymmetry, skin color changes/asymmetry; (3) sudomotor/edema: edema, sweating changes/asymmetry; and (4) motor/trophic: decreased range of motion, weakness, tremor, dystonia, and/or trophic changes to the skin/nails/hair. Patient displays at least 1 sign that is observed at the time of evaluation in 2 or more of the categories above. No other diagnosis better explains the signs and symptoms.

The Valencia consensus adaptations published in 2021 by the International Assosication for the Study of Pain CRPS special interest group clarified ambiguities from Budapest criteria.
Asymmetry is based on clinical judgement rather than prespecified quantitative criteria True spreading of CRPS requires meeting full diagnostic criteria in multiple limbs.
The Budapest criteria serves as the clinical diagnostic standard. No validated tools exist for pediatric CRPS so this is applied to children as well.

History and physical are key for diagnosis. Consider CRPS when pain is disproportionate to trauma or lasts longer than expected. The trauma may be minor; the most common inciting event is a fractured extremity. The pain often starts locally and spreads.

Patients often report skin changes, hair or nail changes, temperature changes, and/or swelling; they may also experience sweating and motor changes. Physical examination can show hyperalgesia, allodynia, skin color changes, decreased motion, tremor, sweating, and edema.

In a series of 74 patients with CRPS, the following symptoms were reported: swelling (97%), color changes (77%), temperature changes (62%), motor deficits (57%), sensory abnormalities (46%), allodynia (54%), and abnormal sweating (28%).

In the same series, physicians found objective evidence of the following signs: swelling (92%), color changes (73%), temperature changes (60%), motor deficits (46%), sensory abnormalities (19%), allodynia (60%), abnormal sweating (24%), and trophic changes (32%).
Use the Budapest criteria (above under Diagnostic Criteria) to confirm the diagnosis clinically.
Imaging and tests (EMG, nerve conduction, MRI, x-ray,) should be used selectively based on the clinical findings. They are primarily used to rule out other conditions.

Tests for CRPS include triple phase bone scan, MRI, radiographs, and thermography.For each test, the sensitivity and negative predictive value are poor, so a normal result does not rule out CRPS. In a prospective study of 158 patients with distal radial fracture, triple phase bone scan at 8 or 16 weeks, radiographs at 8 weeks, and MRI at 16 weeks had reasonably good specificity and positive predictive value when abnormal. Typical abnormalities of each test are described below.
Triple phase bone scans: Findings often show increased uptake in the third stage, cortical thinning, and patchy osteopenia.
MRI:Findings on MRI include marrow edema, increased uptake of contrast at joints and skin.
Thermography: Findings show that thermography is best used to show a difference in thermoregulatory response.

Suspect CRPS in patients who complain of pain that is disproportionate to the initial injury and one or more of the following: swelling, movement disorder, changes in tissue growth, and signs of abnormal functioning of the sympathetic nervous system.
There is limited use for imaging studies and tests. They are primarily used to rule out other conditions.
Imaging studies such as MRI, thermography, radiography, and bone scan can indicate CRPS if abnormal 8 to 16 weeks after injury, but a normal scan does not rule out CRPS.
A multidisciplinary approach is the key. Provide a written treatment plan and initiate safe, simple therapies first such as physical therapy for mobilization. C
Consider offering psychotherapy, especially if there is any underlying mental health disorder. C
Effective treatment options include bisphosphonates, oral corticosteroids and intranasal calcitonin.B
NSAIDs, tricyclic antidepressants, seizure medications (eg, gabapentin and carbamazepine), and opioids are often used. C
Spinal cord stimulation is an effective option but should be considered a treatment of last resort due to its cost and invasiveness. A
Low-dose naltrexone (~4.5 mg daily) is used off-label and is proposed to have immunomodulatory effects, potentially via toll-like receptor 4 antagonism and cytokine modulation. C

There are few good quality studies for treatment for CRPS. As the pathopysiology is still unknown and the diagnosis is based on consensus guideline, it is difficult to research treatment modalities. There are few treatments with good evidence behind them.

An expert review recommends that initial therapy involves reassurance regarding a generally favorable prognosis and use of acetaminophen and NSAIDs but not opioids. If pain persists at 4 weeks, add IV bisphophonate. Second line therapies include tricyclic antidepressants, gabapentinoids and SNRIs. Cognitive behavioral therapy is also effective. For severe long-term pain (> 18 months) consider spinal cord stimulation.

A systematic review concluded that evidence for treatment efficacy is strong for bisphosphonates, and repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation and graded motor imagery. However most trails were small with a short follow up period. Another systematic review of four small randomized controlled trials showed limited data but some potential short-term benefit for bisphosphonates in CRPS. In one RCT, neridronate (a bisphosphonate) given at 100 milligrams IV 4 times over 10 days was associated with a significant 22 millimeter decrease in a 100 mm visual analogue scale (VAS) compared to placebo.
Bisophosphonates (such as a single 60mg intravenous pamidronate infusion) has been shown effective in early CRPS (within 6 months) by 10 points on 100 point scale.

A systematic review of pharmacologic therapy found the best evidence to support bisphosphonates for reducing pain (mean difference 24 points on a 100 point scale compared with placebo). Ketamines were also effective but this must be balanced against potential risks of ketamine therapy. IVIG was not effective.

A systematic review of 21 studies found that most were small and of poor methodologic quality. The review found no evidence from 12 small RCTs that sympathetic suppressing agents such as beta blockers are effective, or from from 6 RCTs that guanethidine is effective.
A protocol with a combination of 20% mannitol given IV along with a steroid and oral gabapentin was associated with recovery of grip strength, pain level of finger range of motion.
An RCT found that prednisolone, 40 mg for 14 days followed by a taper of 10 mg/week, can provide short-term improvement of pain (NNT = 1.5).
Calcitonin nasal spray, 100 IU three times a day, for 3 weeks may provide some relief. A systematic review of 5 studies with 280 patients found a significant benefit.

Opioids and tramadol are also used clinically, but good studies are lacking in patients with CRPS. Opioids should be prescribed cautiously and has an unfavorable risk-benefit profile in CRPS due to adverse effects of developing tolerance and dependency.
Small studies have found benefit from IV ketamine infusions for CRPS-1. A 4-day infusion regimen provided symptom relief during a 12 week follow-up period in 1 study of 60 patients.
While sympathetic blocks have been used, and were considered the gold standard in treatment and diagnosis, there is no good evidence to prove that they are beneficial.

In a Cochrane review of 12 studies (N = 461) judged to be at high or unclear bias, it was concluded that there was a lack of high quality evidence to support or refute the use of local anesthetic blockade in the treatment of complex regional pain syndrome.
A small, non-randomized study found that use of botulinum toxin extended the duration of relief following lumbar sympathetic block.

Spinal cord stimulation through the implantation of an electrical generator that delivers pulses to the targeted spinal cord area has been proposed. A systematic review found limited studies, but it appears to be promising. The potential side effects and expense warrant this as a treatment if no response occurs to other treatment.

The use of surgical or chemical sympathectomy for CRPS and neuropathic pain has very little high quality evidence to support its use. In a small randomized controlled trial of 20 patients treated with surgical or chemical sympathectomy for CRPS, baseline pain scores dropped from a pain scale of 8-9/10 to 3-5/10 after 4 months.
Qigong exercises were shown to offer some benefit in one study. Recommend 40 minutes of exercise twice a week for 4 weeks.
Some patients report pain improvement with cannabidiol oil, but there is limited evidence supporting its use
Acupuncture and DMSO (dimethyl sulfoxide) do not appear to be effective.

Goal is try to improve function; recommend early mobilization, desensitization, strengthening, and hydrotherapy of the affected limb with physical and occupational therapy being the cornerstone of treatment.
Therapy focuses on normalizing skin sensation, gentle limb movement, progressive weight-bearing and functional restoration.
Promising data exist for use of team-based approach with physical therapy, pharmacotherapy, and psychotherapy.
A series of cognitive exercises (graded motor imagery, mirror therapy and exposure-based approaches) performed by specially-trained physical therapists has shown promise in some studies.
Evidence on treatment is limited, but generally, a team approach with psychotherapy, physical therapy, and medications is a good idea.
Treat comorbid conditions such as depression.
Provide a written treatment plan, as it may lessen the confusion and frustration a patient may experience.
Initiate safe, simple therapies first such as physical therapy for mobilization.
Motor cortex stimulation may be helpful in patients with chronic pain, based on a systematic review of 22 studies with only 327 patients.
Early treatment of CRPS is more likely to lead to remission. C
Seventy-four percent of CRPS cases will resolve, often spontaneously. B
Historically CRPS was thought to have 3 stages, but guidelines state that progression is variable and does not follow the stages.
Early stages will often show edema, warmth, pain, and sweating.
Late stages often show atrophy, tremor, cold, and severe pain.
Prognosis of CRPS is variable and unpredictable.
One series of 74 patients found that most patients with CRPS I had resolution of their symptoms.
If identified and treated, early remission is likely in 3 to 6 months. Patients without sensory symptoms and with objective swelling are more likely to recover.
Often untreated patients will note spread of the symptoms and worsening of the symptoms, that can become irreversible.
For patients who suffer long term from CRPS, consider monitoring for development of osteoporosis.
Key to treatment is early mobility and return to normal activities.
For an upper extremity fracture, recommend vitamin C 500 mg once daily, especially ithe patient is older than 40 years.
